title: Bills of Exchange and Promissory Notes
outcomes: Explain what a bill of exchange and a promissory note are, list their essential features and parties, and tell the two apart.
Work out the due date and the date of maturity of any bill — after date, after sight, in months or days, at month-end and on holidays.
Journalise drawing, acceptance, holding, endorsement, discounting, collection, honour and dishonour (with noting charges) in the books of the drawer, drawee and endorsee.
Record renewal with interest, retirement under rebate, and insolvency of the acceptor in both sets of books.
Account for accommodation bills, sharing proceeds and discount correctly, and describe bills receivable and bills payable books.

meta.exam_tip: Examiners ask for entries "in the books of" a named party — read that line twice. Draw a quick time-line of dates (drawing, discounting, maturity) before you journalise; most lost marks come from wrong maturity dates and from debiting the wrong account on dishonour.

concepts.title: Bill of exchange: a written order to pay
body: A bill of exchange is a signed, written instrument in which one person (the drawer, usually the seller) orders another (the drawee, usually the buyer) to pay a fixed sum of money to a named person, to his order, or to the bearer. Once the drawee signs his acceptance on it, he becomes the acceptor and the bill becomes a binding credit instrument.

Essentials: it is in writing and dated; it contains an order (not a request) to pay; the order is unconditional; the amount is certain and in the legal currency of the country; the payee is certain; it is accepted by the drawee; and it carries the stamp duty required (bills payable on demand are an exception).

Parties: drawer (makes the order), drawee/acceptor (who must pay), payee (who receives the money — often the drawer himself). A holder can transfer the bill by endorsement; the acceptor is primarily liable, and if he fails, the holder can claim from the drawer and earlier endorsers.

Foreign bill: under Section 12 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, any instrument that is not an inland instrument is foreign — for example, a bill drawn in India on a person abroad and payable abroad. Foreign bills are usually drawn in a set of three copies sent separately; once one copy is paid the others are of no use.
concepts.analogy: A bill is like a written IOU that the seller writes and the buyer signs — "Pay ₹50,000 in three months" — which the seller can then sell to a bank or pass on to his own supplier like money.
concepts.work: Exporters still draw bills on foreign buyers, and banks finance them. Treasury and accounts teams track every bill receivable by maturity date so that cash planning and follow-up of dues are on time.

concepts.title: Promissory note and how it differs from a bill
body: A promissory note is a signed written instrument (not a bank note or currency note) in which the maker unconditionally promises to pay a fixed amount of money to a named person or as that person directs. Section 31(2) of the RBI Act forbids anyone other than the authorities named there from issuing a promissory note payable to bearer.

Essentials: written; a clear promise (merely admitting a debt is not enough); unconditional ("I will pay when I can" fails); signed by a definite maker to a definite payee; certain amount in legal currency; properly stamped; no acceptance needed.

Maker's liability is primary and absolute

blocks.title: Bill of exchange vs promissory note

concepts.analogy: Bill: "I tell you to pay." Note: "I promise I will pay." The first needs the other person to say yes (accept); the second needs only your own signature.
concepts.work: Lenders often take a demand promissory note from a borrower as extra security. When you audit loans given, you check that such notes exist, are signed by the borrower and are properly stamped.

concepts.title: Recording bills: Bills Receivable and Bills Payable
body: The party who receives an accepted bill (or a promissory note) records a new asset — Bills Receivable: Bills Receivable A/c Dr, To Drawee (customer). The party who accepts a bill (or makes a note) records a new liability — Bills Payable: Creditor A/c Dr, To Bills Payable A/c. The bill does not create a new sale or purchase; it only converts a book debt into a written one.

The holder of a bill receivable has three choices: (1) hold it till maturity — on payment, Bank Dr, To Bills Receivable; (2) endorse it to a creditor — Creditor Dr, To Bills Receivable; (3) discount it with a bank — Bank Dr (net proceeds), Discount on Bills Dr (bank's charge), To Bills Receivable.

On maturity, if the bill is honoured, only the person holding it at that time records receipt. If the drawer had endorsed or discounted it, he passes no entry when it is met. The acceptor always passes: Bills Payable Dr, To Bank.
concepts.analogy: Converting a debtor into a bill receivable is like turning a verbal promise into a signed cheque-like paper — the amount is the same, but now it can be sold (discounted) or handed over (endorsed).
concepts.work: In practice, bank statements show "bills discounted" and "bills returned unpaid". Matching these with the bills register is a routine month-end task in a distributor's accounts department.

concepts.title: Term, due date, days of grace and maturity
body: Term: the period for which the bill runs (usually up to about 90 days). For a bill "after date" the term starts from the date of drawing; for a bill "after sight" it starts from the date of acceptance (sight).

Due date (expiry): the day the term ends. Months: the same date in the later month; if that month has no such date, its last day (a bill dated 31 August for 6 months expires on 28 February in a non-leap year). Days: count forward excluding the date of the bill.

Days of grace: every instrument not payable on demand gets three days of grace. Date of maturity = due date + 3 days. No grace is added for bills payable on demand, at sight or on presentment — these are payable whenever presented. A cheque is always payable on demand and so can never be a time instrument.

Holidays: if the date of maturity is a public holiday, the bill matures on the preceding business day; if it is an emergency (unforeseen) holiday declared later, the next following business day. In exam questions treat a date as a holiday only when the question says so — weekdays are normally ignored, although strictly Section 25 of the Negotiable Instruments Act counts Sundays as public holidays.

blocks.title: Due dates and maturity dates

concepts.analogy: Think of a library book: the due date is stamped inside, but the library lets you return it up to three days late without a fine. Those three days are the days of grace.
concepts.work: Wrong maturity dates lead to wrong discount, interest and rebate figures. Trade-finance desks and accounts teams keep a maturity diary so that bills are presented on time — missing presentment can weaken the right to recover.

concepts.title: Dishonour and noting charges
body: A bill is dishonoured when the acceptor fails to pay on maturity. The bill becomes worthless as an asset, and the acceptor again owes the amount plus any expenses.

Noting: to prove dishonour, the holder gets a notary public to present the bill again and record (note) the fact and reason of dishonour. The notary's fee is noting charges, paid by the holder but recoverable from the party responsible for the dishonour — ultimately the acceptor.

Drawer's entry depends on where the bill is: still held — Drawee Dr (bill + noting), To Bills Receivable and To Bank (noting paid); endorsed — Drawee Dr, To Endorsee (who claims from the drawer); discounted — Drawee Dr, To Bank (the bank debits the drawer). Acceptor's entry: Bills Payable Dr, Noting Charges Dr, To Drawer.
concepts.analogy: If a cheque you deposit bounces, your bank reverses the credit and charges you; you then chase the person who gave it to you for the amount plus the charges. Dishonour of a discounted bill works the same way.
concepts.work: When a customer's bill is returned unpaid, accounts must reverse the receipt, recover noting charges and alert the credit team. Auditors check that dishonoured bills are not still shown as bills receivable.

concepts.title: Renewal of a bill
body: When the acceptor cannot pay on maturity, he may request more time and agree to pay interest for the extension. The old bill is cancelled (recorded exactly like a dishonour) and a new bill is drawn and accepted.

Amount of the new bill: (i) if nothing is paid — old amount + interest; (ii) if interest is paid in cash — old amount only; (iii) if part of the amount (and/or interest) is paid — the unpaid amount plus interest on that unpaid amount for the extended period.
Interest for renewal: Drawer — Drawee Dr, To Interest; Acceptor — Interest Dr, To Drawer.
concepts.analogy: Renewal is like rolling over a fixed-term loan: you close the old contract, add interest for the extra time, and sign a fresh one.
concepts.work: Frequent renewals by the same customer are an early-warning sign of credit stress. A CA reviewing receivables flags them for provisioning discussion with management.

concepts.title: Retirement of a bill under rebate
body: Retiring a bill means the acceptor pays it before the date of maturity. The holder allows a rebate (discount) for the unexpired period — from the date of payment to the date of maturity — at the agreed rate.

Rebate = Amount of bill × rate × unexpired period. For the drawer/holder the rebate is an expense: Bank Dr, Rebate on Bills Dr, To Bills Receivable. For the acceptor it is an income: Bills Payable Dr, To Bank, To Rebate on Bills.
Do not confuse retirement (paying early, earning rebate) with renewal (paying late, bearing interest).
concepts.analogy: Paying your credit card bill before the statement date and getting cash-back for it — early payment earns you a small reward.
concepts.work: Businesses with surplus cash compare the rebate offered with what the money would earn elsewhere. If the rebate rate beats the bank deposit rate, retiring bills early is a sensible treasury decision.

concepts.title: Insolvency of the acceptor
body: If the acceptor becomes insolvent, his acceptance will not be met, so the holder records the dishonour at once (it need not wait for maturity in exams if insolvency is announced). Later, whatever the official assignee pays from the estate is debited to Bank, and the unrecovered balance is written off as Bad Debts.
Work out the amount due from the insolvent first (including any noting charges or interest debited to him), then apply the rate — "40 paise in the rupee" means 40% of the amount due.
In the insolvent acceptor's books, the amount he cannot pay is credited to Deficiency Account (the creditor is debited with the full amount, Bank credited with what is paid).
concepts.analogy: If a friend who owes you ₹1,000 goes bankrupt and the court pays creditors 40 paise per rupee, you get ₹400 and must accept that ₹600 is lost.
concepts.work: When a customer is admitted into insolvency proceedings, the finance team files its claim, stops further credit, and the auditor checks whether the receivable has been written off or provided for.

concepts.title: Accommodation bills
body: An accommodation bill is drawn and accepted without any trade transaction behind it, only to raise funds for one or both parties. The drawer discounts the accepted bill with his bank and uses the money; before maturity he sends the acceptor the amount so the bill can be met.

When both parties need money, the proceeds are shared in an agreed ratio and the discount is borne in the same ratio. Entries are the ordinary bill entries plus: remitting the other party's share of proceeds and charging him his share of discount; and the remittance on maturity.
If one party becomes insolvent, the other must bear the loss: the solvent party writes off the unrecovered amount as bad debts; the insolvent party credits the unpaid amount to Deficiency Account.
concepts.analogy: Two friends each need a short loan. One signs a paper promising to pay; the other takes it to a moneylender, gets cash and splits it. Both share the moneylender's fee in the same ratio as they shared the cash.
concepts.work: Accommodation paper between related parties can be used to window-dress liquidity. Auditors look for bills with no matching sales invoice and for circular bills between group concerns.

concepts.title: Bills sent for collection; bills receivable and payable books
body: Bill for collection: the holder hands the bill to his bank only for safe custody and collection on maturity — not for discounting. The bank credits the account only when it collects. Entries: Bills for Collection Dr, To Bills Receivable; on collection Bank Dr, To Bills for Collection; on dishonour Drawee Dr, To Bills for Collection.

Where bills are many, a Bills Receivable Book and a Bills Payable Book are kept as subsidiary day books. They record each bill's date, party, term, due date, place of payment, amount and how it was disposed of (held, endorsed, discounted, collected). Personal accounts are posted individually; periodic totals go to the Bills Receivable and Bills Payable accounts.
concepts.analogy: Sending a bill for collection is like giving a parcel to a courier for delivery against payment — the courier pays you only after the customer pays it.
concepts.work: A bills register is the first document an auditor asks for when testing bills receivable: bills in hand should agree with the ledger balance, and discounted bills not yet matured are disclosed as a contingent liability.

illustrations.q: Find the date of maturity of each bill: (a) dated 14 January 2027, payable 3 months after date; (b) dated 30 November 2026, payable 3 months after date; (c) dated 10 June 2026, payable 60 days after date; (d) drawn 5 July 2026 and accepted 9 July 2026, payable 2 months after sight; (e) the same bill payable 2 months after date; (f) dated 23 October 2026, payable 3 months after date; (g) a bill payable at sight.

In (f), if the government had instead declared 26 January an emergency holiday at short notice, the bill would mature on the next business day, 27 January 2027.

February 2027 has 28 days; expiry 28 February + 3 days of grace = 3 March

illustrations.title: Discounting, dishonour and renewal — books of both parties
illustrations.q: On 1 January 2027 Neel Traders sold goods for ₹2,40,000 to Prakash and drew on him a bill at 3 months, which he accepted. On 4 January Neel Traders discounted the bill with its bank at 12% p.a. On maturity the bill was dishonoured and the bank paid ₹400 as noting charges. On the same day Prakash paid ₹40,400 in cash and accepted a new bill at 2 months for the balance plus interest at 15% p.a. The new bill was met on maturity. Journalise in the books of Neel Traders and of Prakash, and show Prakash's account in the books of Neel Traders.

entries.narr: Being goods sold on credit to Prakash
Being Prakash's 3-month acceptance received, maturing on 4 April 2027
Being the bill discounted with the bank at 12% p.a. for 3 months
Being the discounted bill dishonoured; bank debited the bill amount and ₹400 noting charges
Being interest @15% p.a. for 2 months on ₹2,00,000 charged for renewal
Being cash received and a new 2-month acceptance (bill + interest) received in renewal
Being the renewed bill met on maturity
Being goods bought on credit from Neel Traders
Being 3-month bill drawn by Neel Traders accepted
Being own acceptance dishonoured; noting charges payable to the drawer
Being interest payable for the extension of 2 months
Being cash paid and a new 2-month bill accepted for the balance with interest
Being the renewed bill paid on maturity

solution.title: Working notes
solution.text: Maturity of first bill: 1 April + 3 days = 4 April 2027. Discount = 2,40,000 × 12% × 3/12 = ₹7,200; proceeds ₹2,32,800. On dishonour Prakash owes ₹2,40,400. Cash ₹40,400 clears the noting charges and ₹40,000 of the bill, leaving ₹2,00,000; interest ₹2,00,000 × 15% × 2/12 = ₹5,000; new bill ₹2,05,000, maturing 4 June + 3 = 7 June 2027.

checks.label: Discount charged by the bank: 12% p.a. for 3 months (4 Jan to 4 Apr) on 2,40,000
Amount due from Prakash on dishonour (bill + noting charges)
Cash paid by Prakash on 4 April (noting charges + part of the bill)
Balance carried into the new bill before interest
Total credited to Prakash on 4 April (cash + new bill)

illustrations.title: Bill sent for collection and a bill retired early
illustrations.q: Sohan owed Ritu ₹1,50,000. On 1 May 2026 Ritu drew two bills on him, which he accepted: Bill A for ₹60,000 at 3 months and Bill B for ₹90,000 at 4 months. On 10 May Ritu sent Bill A to her bank for collection; the bank collected it on maturity. On 4 July Sohan retired Bill B, Ritu allowing a rebate at 10% p.a. Journalise in the books of Ritu and Sohan.

entries.narr: Being two acceptances received from Sohan: Bill A ₹60,000 (3 months) and Bill B ₹90,000 (4 months)
Being Bill A sent to the bank for collection on maturity
Being Bill B retired by Sohan two months before maturity under rebate @10% p.a.
Being Bill A collected by the bank on maturity
Being two bills drawn by Ritu accepted
Being Bill B retired two months early; rebate @10% p.a. earned
Being Bill A paid on maturity

solution.title: Working notes
solution.text: Bill A matures 1 August + 3 = 4 August 2026; Bill B matures 1 September + 3 = 4 September 2026. On 4 July, 2 months remain for Bill B: rebate = 90,000 × 10% × 2/12 = ₹1,500; cash ₹88,500. Sending a bill for collection is not discounting — no discount arises and the bank credits Ritu only on 4 August.

checks.label: Rebate @10% p.a. for the unexpired 2 months (4 July to 4 September)
Cash paid by Sohan on retiring Bill B

illustrations.title: Accommodation bill ending in insolvency
illustrations.q: On 1 June 2026 Asha drew a 3-month bill for ₹1,20,000 on Bimal for their mutual accommodation; Bimal accepted it. Asha discounted it the same day for ₹1,17,000 and remitted half the proceeds to Bimal, the discount to be shared equally. Before maturity Asha became insolvent, so Bimal met the bill himself on maturity. Asha's estate paid 40 paise in the rupee on 4 September. Journalise in both books.

entries.narr: Being Bimal's acceptance received for mutual accommodation
Being the bill discounted with the bank
Being half the proceeds remitted to Bimal and half the discount charged to him
Being 40% of the amount due to Bimal paid by the official assignee; the unpaid 60% credited to Deficiency Account
Being bill drawn by Asha accepted for mutual accommodation
Being half the proceeds received; half the discount borne
Being own acceptance met on maturity
Being 40 paise in the rupee received from Asha's estate; the balance written off

solution.title: Working notes
solution.text: Discount ₹3,000; each bears ₹1,500. Bimal receives ₹58,500 cash and is charged ₹1,500 discount, so ₹60,000 of the bill is his own. He meets ₹1,20,000, so Asha owes him ₹60,000. Recovery 40% = ₹24,000; loss ₹36,000 — bad debts for Bimal, deficiency for Asha.

checks.label: Bimal's half share of the proceeds
Bimal's half share of the discount
Amount Asha owes Bimal after he meets the bill
Recovered from Asha's estate (40 paise in the rupee)

jobs.title: A discounted bill comes back unpaid
jobs.role: Accounts executive at a building-materials distributor
jobs.situation: The bank statement shows a debit of ₹3,00,750 marked "bill returned unpaid — incl. charges ₹750" against a dealer's bill you had discounted last quarter. The dealer phones asking for a 60-day extension.
steps: Pass the dishonour entry: Dealer Dr ₹3,00,750, To Bank ₹3,00,750 — the bank has already recovered the money from you.
Tell sales and credit control; stop further supplies on credit until the matter is settled.
If management agrees to renew, get a fresh acceptance for the agreed amount including interest for 60 days, and record the interest income.
Update the bills register: original bill marked "dishonoured/renewed", new bill entered with its maturity date.
At year end, judge whether a provision is needed if the dealer has a history of renewals.
jobs.takeaway: A discounted bill is not "money in the bank" until it is met — the drawer stays liable to the bank until maturity.
jobs.think: Why do auditors want discounted but unmatured bills disclosed in the notes to accounts?
jobs.answer: Because if any of them is dishonoured, the bank will recover the money from the business — a contingent liability that readers must know about.

jobs.title: Year-end verification of bills receivable
jobs.role: Articled assistant on a statutory audit
jobs.situation: The client's ledger shows Bills Receivable of ₹8,40,000 at 31 March. You are asked to verify it.
steps: Get the bills receivable book and list bills not disposed of at 31 March.
Physically inspect bills in hand; for bills with the bank for collection, obtain the bank's confirmation.
Check that bills discounted or endorsed have been removed from the balance and are listed for contingent-liability disclosure.
Look at April receipts: bills met after the year end support the balance; bills dishonoured in April may need a provision.
Recompute a sample of maturity dates and discount amounts.
jobs.takeaway: The bills register, physical bills, bank confirmations and post-year-end receipts together prove the balance.
jobs.think: A bill for ₹50,000 sent for collection on 25 March is shown as "Bank" instead of "Bills Receivable" at 31 March. What is wrong?
jobs.answer: A bill sent for collection is not cash until the bank collects it. Until then it remains an asset (Bills for Collection / Bills Receivable), not a bank balance.

mcqs.q: A bill dated 20 January 2027 is payable 3 months after date. Its date of maturity is:
mcqs.explain: A bill 'after date' runs from the date of drawing, so 3 months after 20 January expires on 20 April. Add the three days of grace that every time bill gets: the bill matures on 23 April 2027. The tempting 20 April is only the due (expiry) date — forgetting the grace days is the trap. In practice: an accounts assistant at a Surat textile trader diarises each bill's maturity date so it is presented to the customer's bank on exactly the right day.
mcqs.topic: Term, due date, days of grace and maturity

mcqs.q: A bill dated 15 February 2027 is payable 90 days after date. It matures on:
mcqs.explain: When the term is in days, exclude the date of the bill and count forward: 13 days left in February 2027 (16th–28th) + 31 in March + 30 in April = 74, so 16 more days in May make 90. The bill expires on 16 May; add three days of grace to get 19 May 2027. Stopping at 16 May forgets grace; counting 15 February itself gives a day early. In practice: trade-finance staff at banks run these day-counts daily before presenting usance bills.
mcqs.topic: Term, due date, days of grace and maturity

mcqs.q: A bill dated 31 October 2026 is drawn for 4 months after date. The date of maturity is:
mcqs.explain: Four months after 31 October falls in February 2027, which has no 31st. The rule is to take the last day of that month, so the bill expires on 28 February (2027 is not a leap year). Add three days of grace: 1, 2, 3 March — maturity is 3 March 2027. The trap is stopping at 28 February, which is only the expiry date. In practice: month-end bills are common in wholesale trade, and getting the February rule wrong shifts the interest and presentment date.
mcqs.topic: Term, due date, days of grace and maturity

mcqs.q: A bill of ₹1,80,000 is retired 2 months before maturity under a rebate of 12% p.a. The rebate is:
mcqs.explain: Rebate is allowed only for the unexpired period, from the date of payment to the date of maturity: 1,80,000 × 12% × 2/12 = ₹3,600. The tempting ₹21,600 applies the 12% for a full year, forgetting that the rate is per annum and the bill is paid just two months early. In practice: a distributor with surplus cash compares this rebate with what a bank fixed deposit would earn before deciding to retire its acceptances early.
mcqs.topic: Retirement of a bill under rebate

mcqs.q: A 4-month bill of ₹75,000 is discounted one month after drawing at 16% p.a. The bank pays:
mcqs.explain: The bank charges discount only for the period it waits — from the date of discounting to maturity. The bill already ran one month, so 3 months remain: 75,000 × 16% × 3/12 = ₹3,000, and the bank pays 75,000 − 3,000 = ₹72,000. The trap is charging for the full 4 months (₹4,000), giving ₹71,000. In practice: MSMEs discount customers' bills with banks (or on the TReDS platforms) and the discount charged always depends on the days left to maturity.
mcqs.topic: Recording bills: Bills Receivable and Bills Payable

mcqs.q: A bill discounted with the bank is dishonoured on maturity. In the drawer's books the entry is:
options: Drawee A/c Dr. To Bank A/c
Drawee A/c Dr. To Bills Receivable A/c
Bills Receivable A/c Dr. To Bank A/c
Bank A/c Dr. To Drawee A/c
mcqs.explain: Once a bill is discounted, Bills Receivable is already closed. On dishonour the bank recovers the amount from the drawer by debiting his account (credit Bank), and the drawee again owes the drawer (debit Drawee). Crediting Bills Receivable is the trap — that account no longer holds the bill. In practice: when a discounted bill is 'returned unpaid', the drawer's bank statement shows a debit, and the accountant reinstates the customer's dues in the debtors ledger.

mcqs.q: As per Section 31(2) of the RBI Act, a promissory note made by a trader:
options: Cannot be made payable to bearer
mcqs.explain: Section 31(2) of the RBI Act allows only the RBI (and, in limited cases, the Central Government) to issue promissory notes payable to bearer, because such notes would work like currency. So a trader's note cannot be payable to bearer. The tempting 'needs acceptance' is wrong — acceptance is a feature of bills; a note is the maker's own promise. In practice: banks take demand promissory notes from borrowers payable to the bank itself, never to bearer, as loan documentation.
mcqs.topic: Promissory note and how it differs from a bill

mcqs.q: In the books of the acceptor, rebate received on retiring a bill is:
options: An income, credited to Rebate on Bills
An expense, debited to Rebate on Bills
mcqs.explain: The acceptor pays less than the face value of his bill by retiring it early. The saving is a gain for him, so in his books Rebate on Bills is credited and treated as income. The trap is 'an expense, debited' — that is the treatment in the holder's (drawer's) books, who gives up part of the amount. In practice: a buyer company's accounts team books such early-payment rebates as other income, much like cash discount received from suppliers.
mcqs.topic: Retirement of a bill under rebate

mcqs.q: In the books of an insolvent acceptor, the part of a bill he is unable to pay is credited to:
mcqs.explain: An insolvent acceptor cannot pay the full amount. In his own books the creditor is debited with the full sum, Bank is credited with what is actually paid, and the unpaid part is credited to Deficiency Account. Bad Debts Account is the tempting answer, but that is used by the creditor (the drawer) who loses the money, not by the debtor. In practice: under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, creditors file claims and later write off what the resolution process does not recover.

mcqs.q: Days of grace are NOT added in the case of a bill:
mcqs.explain: Days of grace are allowed only to time instruments — bills payable after a fixed period. A bill payable at sight (or on demand or presentment) is due the moment it is presented, so no grace is added. Bills '60 days after sight' or '2 months after acceptance' are time bills: their term begins at sight, but they still get three days of grace — that is the trap. In practice: exporters using sight bills under letters of credit receive payment when documents are presented, with no grace period.
mcqs.topic: Term, due date, days of grace and maturity

mcqs.q: An accommodation bill of ₹2,00,000 is discounted for ₹1,94,000; the drawer and drawee share the proceeds 3 : 1. The drawee's share of discount is:
mcqs.explain: Discount = 2,00,000 − 1,94,000 = ₹6,000. In an accommodation bill the discount is shared in the same ratio as the proceeds, here 3 : 1. The drawee's share is 6,000 × 1/4 = ₹1,500 and the drawer's ₹4,500. The trap is splitting the discount equally (₹3,000) or giving the drawee the larger share. In practice: accommodation bills between related firms are watched by auditors because they raise funds without any underlying sale.

mcqs.q: A ₹1,00,000 bill is renewed: the acceptor pays ₹20,000 in cash and accepts a new 3-month bill for the balance with interest at 12% p.a. The new bill is for:
mcqs.explain: Of the ₹1,00,000 due, ₹20,000 is paid in cash, so only ₹80,000 is extended. Interest is charged only on the unpaid amount: 80,000 × 12% × 3/12 = ₹2,400. New bill = 80,000 + 2,400 = ₹82,400. The trap is charging interest on the full ₹1,00,000 (₹3,000), giving ₹83,000. In practice: repeated renewals by a customer are an early warning of credit stress, which a CA flags while reviewing receivables for provisioning.

mcqs.q: A bill endorsed by A to his creditor C is dishonoured and C pays noting charges. In A's books the entry is:
options: Drawee A/c Dr. To Bills Receivable A/c
Bills Receivable A/c Dr. To C
mcqs.explain: The endorsee C paid noting charges and will claim the bill amount plus noting from A, who endorsed it — so C is credited. A in turn recovers everything from the drawee, who caused the dishonour — so the drawee is debited. Crediting Bills Receivable is the trap: it was already closed when A endorsed the bill to C. In practice: when a customer's paper passed to a supplier bounces, the supplier simply reclaims it, and the accountant reinstates the customer's dues.

mcqs.q: A bill is sent to the bank "for collection". The entry is:
options: Bills for Collection A/c Dr. To Bills Receivable A/c
Bank A/c Dr. To Bills Receivable A/c
Bank A/c Dr. Discount A/c Dr. To Bills Receivable A/c
mcqs.explain: A bill sent 'for collection' is not discounted — the bank only holds it and collects on maturity, so no cash is received yet. The bill is moved from Bills Receivable to Bills for Collection. Debiting Bank now is the trap: the bank credits the account only after collection. In practice: at year-end, auditors check that bills lodged with the bank for collection are shown as receivables, not as bank balance, until the bank's credit advice arrives.
mcqs.topic: Bills sent for collection; bills receivable and payable books

questions.q: On 1 August 2026 Lalit sold goods to Mohan for ₹1,50,000 and drew on him a 3-month bill, which Mohan accepted. On 5 August Lalit endorsed the bill to his creditor Nikhil in full settlement of ₹1,52,000 due to him. On maturity the bill was dishonoured and Nikhil paid ₹300 as noting charges; Lalit settled Nikhil's claim by cheque. On the same day Mohan paid ₹30,300 in cash and accepted a new 3-month bill for the balance plus interest at 12% p.a. Before the new bill matured Mohan became insolvent and 60 paise in the rupee was received from his estate on its maturity date. Pass journal entries in the books of Lalit.

Being Mohan's 3-month acceptance received (maturity 4 November 2026)
Being Mohan's acceptance endorsed to Nikhil in full settlement of ₹1,52,000
Being the endorsed bill dishonoured; Nikhil paid ₹300 noting charges
Being Nikhil paid by cheque for the dishonoured bill and noting charges
Being interest @12% p.a. for 3 months on ₹1,20,000 charged for renewal
Being cash and a new 3-month acceptance received from Mohan
Being Mohan's renewed acceptance dishonoured on his insolvency
Being 60 paise in the rupee received from his estate and the balance written off

scheme.pt: Dishonour of new bill on insolvency

remarks: Many candidates credit Bills Receivable on dishonour of an endorsed bill — the bill left the books on 5 August, so the endorsee (Nikhil) is credited.
Interest is frequently charged on ₹1,50,300 instead of the unpaid ₹1,20,000.
Good answers show maturity dates in narrations and a short working note for interest and recovery.
mistakes: Ignoring the discount received of ₹2,000 on endorsement.
Writing off 60% instead of 40% as bad debts.
Debiting Noting Charges Account in Lalit's books instead of charging them to Mohan.

Gita accepted it and Farhan discounted it for ₹78,000, remitting one-fourth of the proceeds to Gita. The discount is to be borne in the ratio of the proceeds. On maturity Farhan remitted the amount due to Gita, who met the bill. Journalise in the books of Farhan and Gita.

Being the bill discounted

Being amount remitted to Gita to meet the bill
Being accommodation bill accepted

Being Farhan's remittance received

model.title: Working notes
model.text: Discount ₹2,000: Gita bears 1/4 = ₹500; proceeds to Gita ₹19,500. Gita has used ₹20,000 of the bill, so Farhan must provide ₹60,000 on maturity (4 December 2026).

Write the sharing ratio in a working note.

summary: Bill = order to pay (drawer, drawee, payee; needs acceptance). Promissory note = promise to pay (maker, payee; no acceptance; never to bearer — s.31(2) RBI Act).
Receiver records Bills Receivable (asset); acceptor records Bills Payable (liability).
Holder may hold, endorse or discount the bill; on dishonour the drawee is debited and the account that "has" the bill (B/R, endorsee or bank) is credited.
Maturity = due date + 3 days of grace (none for demand/sight bills). After date runs from drawing; after sight from acceptance. Public holiday → preceding business day.
Renewal: cancel old bill like dishonour, charge interest, take new bill. Retirement: early payment, rebate is the acceptor's income and the holder's expense.
Insolvency: drawer writes off unrecovered amount as bad debts; insolvent drawee credits Deficiency A/c. Accommodation bills share discount in the ratio of proceeds.
remember: Noting charges always end up on the drawee.
Interest on renewal is on the unpaid amount for the extended period only.
Bills for collection ≠ discounting — no discount, no cash until collected.
traps: Don't credit Bills Receivable on dishonour of a bill that was endorsed or discounted.
Don't count the date of the bill when the term is in days.
Don't charge discount for the full term if the bill is discounted after some days have passed.

viva.q: How does a bill of exchange differ from a promissory note?
viva.model: A bill of exchange contains an order to pay, while a promissory note contains a promise to pay. A bill is drawn by the creditor and normally has three parties: drawer, drawee and payee. A promissory note is made by the debtor and has only two parties, the maker and the payee. A bill must be accepted by the drawee, but a promissory note does not need acceptance. A promissory note cannot be made payable to bearer.

viva.q: What are days of grace, and how do you find the date of maturity of a bill?
viva.model: Days of grace are three extra days allowed to the acceptor. The due date is found from the term of the bill, and three days of grace are added to it to get the date of maturity. Days of grace are not added for a bill payable on demand or at sight. If the date of maturity is a public holiday, the bill matures on the preceding business day.

viva.q: A trader has received an accepted bill. What can he do with it, and what entry is passed in each case?
viva.model: He has three options. He can hold the bill till maturity and collect the money, passing Bank Account debit and Bills Receivable credit on payment. He can endorse it to a creditor, debiting the creditor and crediting Bills Receivable. Or he can discount it with a bank, debiting Bank with the proceeds and Discount Account with the discount, and crediting Bills Receivable.

viva.q: What are noting charges, and who finally bears them?
viva.model: Noting charges are the fee paid to a notary public for recording the fact and reason of dishonour of a bill. They are paid by the holder, but they are recoverable from the drawee or acceptor who caused the dishonour, so in the drawer's books the drawee's account is debited with the bill amount plus noting charges.

viva.q: What is an accommodation bill, and how is the discount shared?
viva.model: An accommodation bill is drawn and accepted only to help one or both parties raise funds, not for any trade transaction. The bill is discounted with a bank and the proceeds are shared as agreed. The discount is borne by the parties in the same ratio in which they share the proceeds, and on maturity each party sends the acceptor his share so the bill can be met.

viva.q: How is the insolvency of an acceptor recorded in the books of the drawer and the drawee?
viva.model: In the drawer's books the acceptance is first treated as dishonoured, so the drawee's account is debited. Whatever is received from his estate is debited to Bank, and the unrecovered amount is written off as bad debts. In his own books the insolvent drawee credits Deficiency Account with the amount he is unable to pay.

cases.title: Om Electricals — a bill that went wrong
cases.case: On 1 October 2026 Om Electricals sold goods for ₹3,00,000 to Varun and drew on him a bill for 3 months, which Varun accepted the same day. On 4 October Om Electricals discounted the bill with its bank at 10% per annum. On the date of maturity the bill was dishonoured and the bank paid noting charges of ₹600. Varun then paid ₹1,50,600 in cash and, for the balance, accepted a new bill for 2 months carrying interest at 12% per annum, included in the bill.

mcqs.q: On what date does the original bill mature?
mcqs.explain: The bill is payable 3 months after date and was drawn on 1 October 2026, so it expires on 1 January 2027. Adding three days of grace gives a date of maturity of 4 January 2027. The tempting 1 January is only the expiry date; 7 January wrongly adds grace twice. In practice: the accounts team of an electricals dealer keeps a bills diary sorted by maturity date so that discounted and held bills are followed up on time.
mcqs.topic: Term, due date, days of grace and maturity

mcqs.q: How much does the bank credit to Om Electricals on 4 October?
mcqs.explain: The bank charges discount from 4 October to the maturity date of 4 January — 3 months: 3,00,000 × 10% × 3/12 = ₹7,500. Proceeds credited = 3,00,000 − 7,500 = ₹2,92,500. The tempting ₹3,00,000 forgets that the bank keeps its discount upfront; ₹2,70,000 charges a full year's 10%. In practice: a bank's bill-discounting advice shows the face value, the discount deducted and the net amount credited, which the accountant records as Bank and Discount on Bills debits.
mcqs.topic: Recording bills: Bills Receivable and Bills Payable

mcqs.q: On dishonour, what entry does Om Electricals pass?
options: Varun Dr. ₹3,00,600 To Bills Receivable A/c ₹3,00,600
mcqs.explain: Because the bill was discounted, the bank debits Om Electricals with the bill amount plus ₹600 noting charges = ₹3,00,600, so Bank is credited. Varun, who caused the dishonour, now owes all of it — debit Varun ₹3,00,600. Crediting Bills Receivable is the trap: that account was closed on discounting. Debiting only ₹3,00,000 forgets the noting charges. In practice: a notary's noting fee on a dishonoured bill is always recovered from the defaulting customer.

mcqs.q: What is the amount of the new bill?
mcqs.explain: Varun owes ₹3,00,600. His cash of ₹1,50,600 clears the ₹600 noting charges and ₹1,50,000 of the bill, leaving ₹1,50,000. Interest for 2 months at 12%: 1,50,000 × 12% × 2/12 = ₹3,000. New bill = 1,50,000 + 3,000 = ₹1,53,000. The trap ₹1,53,600 leaves the noting charges unpaid and adds them again. In practice: when renewing a customer's bill, the credit team agrees exactly which dues the cash clears before fixing the new bill amount.
